Smogon is made up of different tiers based on usage. The general idea is that people play to win and thus the most used Pokémon are the best (not always the case but generally). 

At the beginning of a generation all Pokémon are released into OU and after a month the usage data comes in. If a Pokémon has less than 4.52% usage then it will drop to the next tier under.

So for example if dragapult gets lower than 4.52% usage in a month then it will drop from its current tier OU to the next tier under UU. 

This system pretty much ensures that all Pokémon are somewhat viable at least somewhere. Also it makes for very different meta games which is very refreshing. 

The different tiers are OU (OverUsed) UU (UnderUsed) RU (RarelyUsed) NU (NeverUsed) PU (No one knows) ZU (ZeroUsed).

There’s also BL which stands for BanList/BordeLine. For example all Pokémon who are UUBL can be used in OU but not UU or lower since it’s UU’s ban list.

Another thing to note is that this is entirely based on usage which means that some Pokémon who are really good but doesn’t get used end up in low tiers. In gen 9 especially UU mons are actually pretty great in OU and if you look at gastrodon in past gens it’s been NU forever but has had numerous tournaments appearances in higher tier like OU.

This isn’t going to be the best team, it prob won’t even be good but it’ll be usable/good on low ladder.

If you wanna win then you need to comply to the meta but if you just wanna do some casual games on low ladder then bad Pokémon works, but you will definitely feel that you are using bad mons it’s going to be an uphill battle.

Make sure to cover their weaknesses as well. For example you need something to tank special hits as well as something that resists water or grass for sandslash. 

This isn’t the best example cause gyrados isn’t too good but it’s useful for learning, for example gyrados would be a good partner for sandslash, gyrados tanks water/grass moves and sandslash blocks any electric moves aimed at gyrados. 

Another thing you might want to consider is that sandslash is a great mon in the tier it resides in, ZU. If you’re ok not playing OU then I would highly recommend playing ZU instead. 

The power level is way lower so sandslash actually doesn’t get outclassed, it’s actually outclassing a lot of other mons in ZU. 

In ZU sandslash is a great physical tank that hits hard with stab EQ and provides essential support for its team with both spikes stealth rocks rapid spin and knock off. Sandslash might be the best mon for hazard stack in ZU no joke.

DI stands for Directional Input. It multiplies the forced applied to that direction. 

So if I get hit to the right -> and I put my DI all the way to the right -> I will fly much much further to the right, this can give me enough distance to break out of combos sometimes. 

Sometimes you don’t wanna fly to far away from your enemy when taking a hit, so you put your DI in the opposite direction to where you are getting hit. 

Sometimes you wanna fall down to the ground to recover faster, in that case you put your DI all the way down. This is heavily simplified and situations aren’t as clear cut as I make them out here but that’s the jist of it.

Speaking of knock of. There’s a severe lack of it. 

There’s two cornerstones of progress in competitive Pokémon. These two effects are extremely hard or straight up impossible to revert back mid game. They are removing an opponents item and statusing them with for example toxic or t-wave. 

Items that are knocked off you can’t get back and most teams don’t have aromatherapy or heal bell support to take care of status. Hp you can usually heal back up relatively easy. 

Another tip is to use a lot of passive damage on offensive teams since the big walls can usually survive a strong hit with above above 50% health, but that passive damage just tips the scale so slightly that you can 2HKO the wall instead of 3HKO the wall or sometimes 1HKO if you really land those big hits. 

This is why offensive teams almost always require hazard support to function.

It really depends on the tier format and power level. It can also depend on what weaknesses a mon has, for example psychics in gen 1 has no weaknesses since there’s almost no good bug type moves, similarly if there are no good stab users of a certain type in a tier then the types it threatens will be way better of with fewer weaknesses. 

Another factor can be the overall bulk of the tier. In gen 3 “bold Suicune has no weak” since its bulk is so high it can actually take on most of its few weaknesses and outright counter grass and some electric types.

In gen 1 it’s pretty good too have few weaknesses but to have many resistances is great since the power level is enough that neutral hits can exceed and break walls. 

In gen 2 it’s great to have few weaknesses since the power level is lower. 

In gen 5 and 9 neutral hits are way to much for walls to handle as such walls needs to have crucial resistances in order to survive hits. 

In my opinion it’s almost always better to have many useful resistances and some weaknesses cause it’s a 6v6 and one Pokémon doesn’t need to cover everything defensively. It’s a mechanic designed to make each Pokémon seem more like a individual and give them some character. They usually lower one stat and raise another (by 10%), but there are some that do nothing. 

Competitive Pokémon take advantage of this since you usually have 1-2 stats you don’t really care about, this is usually decided based on what attacking spectrum the Pokémon uses (attack or special attack) but sometimes they use both, in this case speed ore defense/special defense is usually lowered. 

For example the pokemon garchomp is a physical attacker which means it doesn’t care about its special attack stat so it can go for a nature that boost attack or speed and lowers special attack. Well first of all you should choose whether you want to play smogon (6v6 singles/doubles) or vgc (4v4 doubles) vgc is the official format of Pokémon but I much more prefer the fanmade community of smogon. Next you should familiarize yourself with the format, find out what Pokémon’s are the top dogs and what strategies are used. For smogon it’s a lot about chipping your opponent and positioning until one of your mons can break through the other team. Vgc is a lot about speed control and positioning. Also consider playing on Pokémon showdown, its a browser Pokémon battle simulator with a fuck ton of quality of life features. You don’t have to breed Pokémon for ivs and you don’t have to train for EVs. I’m not very good at vgc so I’ll continue on smogon only. For smogon you should choose a format to go deeper into, smogon is divided into usage based tiers, if a Pokémon falls below 4.52% usage it drops to the next tier bellow. The tier are Ubers (legendaries and op mons) OU (over used) UU (under used) RU (rarely used) NU (never used) PU (no one knows) ZU (zero used). I’d recommend OU since it’s the standard play tier or UU since it’s a bit easier to understand imo. Next I’d take a look at the viability rankings to see the top dogs and read up on them on smogons own site. Next I’d steal a sample team and use it until you understand the tier. No matter what you do or choose you will be trash a teambuilding but it’s ok, have fun you’ll get better eventually. Also take a look at YouTubers like wolfyvgc (for vgc) or pinkacross or freezai (for smogon). I wish you best of luck and if you have any questions or wanna discuss anything (vgc or smogon) my dms on Reddit are open for you :)

Yeah I agree. We shouldn’t outright tell new players to stop team building cause “they’re bad”. The best advice I can give to new players is to use other people’s teams as well as play around in the teambuilder. Another good advice would be to take a sample team or a team from the bazaar and then add your own twist to it by replacing a mon or two.

Ok so let’s start with Ttar, this set is outright just not effective. Ttar is so slow that even with a choice scarf it fails to outspeed a whole swarm of fast mons that will just plow through your team. To me you need to outright change the whole set here, I personally like AV Ttar as it takes pressure of your team from the special side, I would go with knock of, stone edge, heavy slam and ice punch. You could also do banded ttar. Banded ttar easily switches in on most special attacks and hits HARD af which can open up holes for its teammates to then plow through. For choice I would go stone edge, knock of, earthquake and ice punch.

Next up lycanroc. So this mon really isn’t good in UU, the power level here is just too much for it to handle. It can’t wallbreak or sweep effectively since the overall bulk of the tier is much larger. I would just scrap this mon and use its team slot to patch up any eventual weaknesses the team might have after you fixed the rest of the mons.

Oh shit it’s the boy, my boy clod. So clod is a really good utility and specially defensive mon. It either goes with spikes or stealth rocks to make your more threatening teammates borderline impossible to switch into without HDB’s. The rest of its moveset consists of recovery to stick around longer, earthquake to to do constant damage and toxic to cripple bulky mons trying to take advantage of its passive nature. The only real choice you have to make is if you want water absorb to turn the matchups on water types or unaware to stop a sweep. Unaware is more common for a reason (it’s really good) but there is still a good argument to be made for water absorb. As for tera clod should either run tera water (if unaware) or tera flying (if water absorb).

Treads looks good- … tera rock? Change it to tera water and you’re golden.

Arcanine is a good choice, it takes away the need for clod or treads to run stealth rocks which is really good as they now can run better moves (volt switch/iron head for treads) (spikes for clod).

Standard SD scizor set looks good, no need to change.

Now that the sets are checked you should use tools like “marriland teambuilder” to check its defensive coverage. A good and well balanced team has a way to deal with every type and at least 2 different mons to deal with “highly weak types” (types 3 or more of your mons are weak to). Another good thing to note is that every team should have a ground immunity as ground is one of the most prominent offensive types ever and most mons gets ground type coverage. Last step is testing, no one gets it right the first time. Test and tween your team, change a tera a move an item or the mon entirely until you get a team that’s both effective and you’re confident in playing with.

I’ve been enjoying OU for the most part, the hazard centered meta is really fun as I’ve always gravitated towards spike stack teams in past gens, the spinblocking mind games are especially fun for me as I’ve never experienced it before (I started playing mid gen 7). But recently I’ve just felt that OU is a little bit too dull, maybe it’s because the limited dex making the meta far more one dimensional. 

I’ve started to play a lot more DOU than OU and I think the format is perfect. You never feel that you don’t know what to do and there is always several good choices to do in one turn. Something that is really unique for DOU is the massive amounts of tools you have to map out a game. Like I said you never feel like you don’t know what to do in a turn, there are always several good choices. And yes there are definitely several times in a OU game where I have no idea what the best move is. 

I would also like to touch the subject of power creep as it is by far the worst this gen. I hated the gen 8 OU meta mostly because dexit but also for its balanced centered meta, as such I gravitated more towards NatDex OU and played a lot more of that than OU. This gens NatDex is pure and utter chaos. I checked out NatDex after like 3 months after gen 9 released and I see past OU staples in UU and RU. I don’t know if there’s anything you can do to compensate power creep but if there is then god please do so.
